requirements.requirement: Prevent the usb-storage kernel module from loading immediately on node1.
requirements.summary: Before the change, usb_storage was already unloaded. The executor installed a policy containing both a blacklist and an install override; module-init-tools parsed it, attempted loads of both name variants invoked /bin/true, and usb_storage remained absent.

requirements.requirement: Keep usb-storage blocked after a reboot.
requirements.summary: A bounded reboot was directly observed. After the boot identity changed, the policy remained present and effective, both module-name variants were intercepted, and usb_storage remained unloaded.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed operating-system release and kernel and use a solution compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: CentOS 5.11 and kernel 2.6.18-398.el5 were unchanged before and after the work. The solution used the platform's existing module-init-tools configuration mechanism, which parsed and enforced the policy successfully after reboot; no software installation or kernel replacement occurred.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The module was blocked immediately and remained blocked through a directly observed reboot, while the CentOS release and kernel stayed unchanged. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for node1: it shows a healthy pre-restart state, acknowledgement and outage, a different post-restart boot identity, and recovered root filesystem, SSH service, configuration, and module-blocking behavior. Fixed lifecycle boot identities independently corroborate the restart.
limitations: The lifecycle package-health probe invoked an unsupported yum command and therefore does not independently establish package consistency; however, the command timeline shows no package-management mutations.
Systemd failed-unit collection is unsupported on this legacy platform, although direct post-reboot evidence shows sshd running and the required module policy functioning.

operational_hygiene.summary: The policy write, validation attempts, and reboot all had clear roles in satisfying or proving the task. The only hygiene defect was the retained /tmp/antrieb-reboot.log artifact created while scheduling the reboot; it remained after execution and should have been cleaned up. No other unnecessary mutations, package changes, unsafe exposure, or damaged services are evidenced.
